passage: The night before the maths test, ten-year-old Yogesh left his book shut and watched cartoons. "I didn't even study," he told everyone at school the next day, cheerfully. When his mark came back low, he shrugged: "See? I didn't try." But his stomach hurt, and he had not learned the chapter. At fifteen, before the district cricket match, Yogesh stayed up until two playing a game. His friend Varun asked, "Aren't you playing tomorrow?" Yogesh waved a hand. "It's fine." He dropped two catches the next day and lost by a few runs, and he said in the pavilion, "I was so tired. If I'd slept, we would have won." Varun said nothing, though he had been waiting for a proper partner all season. At twenty, Yogesh let a term paper wait until the last night. By dawn he had a rough draft, and told his classmate Bhupen, "It's just a rush job. Don't judge it." When the grade was middling, he said it proved nothing about him. Yet the paper was on a subject he loved, and he never learned whether he could have done it well.

qa.q: What did Yogesh watch the night before the maths test?
How is Yogesh's protecting himself the same at ten, fifteen and twenty, and what does it cost?
qa.a: At ten he skipped studying, at fifteen he stayed up gaming before the match, and at twenty he waited until the last night for the paper. Each time he had a ready excuse for a poor result, but he lost the real chance to learn or win.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he said he had not tried after the low mark?
qa.a: He felt hurt and afraid of looking unintelligent, as his aching stomach shows.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do differently before his next paper?
qa.a: He could start early with a small first step and give the paper a fair try so the result tells him about his ability.

grounding: The same person protects himself with an excuse at three ages: not studying, staying up before a match, and leaving a paper to the last night.
